passage: Last spring I nearly bought a used scooter from Wasim, a mechanic two streets from my PG. "Eighty-five thousand, madam, almost new," he said, patting the seat. My first thought was that seventy-five would be a steal. Then I caught myself. Why seventy-five? Only because he'd said eighty-five. So I asked myself a different question: if I had walked in and seen this scooter with no price on it, what would I think it was worth? I honestly didn't know. That evening I checked two resale listings for the same model and year, and asked my cousin, who sells bikes in Nagpur. All three said around sixty. I offered sixty-two. Wasim grumbled, then agreed. I'm Devika, and I still ride it.

qa.q: How much did Wasim first ask for the scooter?
qa.a: Wasim asked for eighty-five thousand.

qa.q: Why did Devika stop herself after thinking seventy-five would be a steal?
qa.a: She noticed that seventy-five only felt fair because Wasim had said eighty-five, and she didn't want his number deciding the price for her.

qa.q: Which of Devika's steps could someone copy when a seller names a price?
qa.a: Ask what the item would be worth with no price on it, then get two or three separate comparisons, like listings and someone in the trade, before making an offer.

qa.q: How might Wasim see Devika's offer of sixty-two?
qa.a: Wasim probably grumbled because the high opening didn't work this time, but an offer backed by the market was hard to argue with.

grounding: Shows a young woman setting aside a seller's first price by imagining the scooter unpriced and gathering three independent comparisons before offering.

passage:
Supervisor's note, purchase team, Friday. Written by Arnab.
Kalyani handled her first laptop order for the new interns this week. The supplier opened with one lakh ten thousand per unit and called it a "special rate". I expected her to bargain down from there, as most new staff do. Instead she said she would reply by Monday. In her working file I later saw a line: "What would I pay if I'd never heard 1.1?" Under it she had three separate quotes: a second supplier, the government purchase portal price, and our own order from last year. All sat near eighty-two thousand. She went back with eighty-three and her reasons. The deal closed at eighty-four. Next step: I have asked her to show the method at the team meeting.

qa.q: What rate did the supplier call a "special rate"?
qa.a: The supplier called one lakh ten thousand per unit a special rate.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani ask for time until Monday instead of bargaining at once?
qa.a: Kalyani seems to have felt wary of the supplier's "special rate" and wanted to step away from that figure so it wouldn't set her starting point. Asking for time let her calmly find out what the laptops were really worth first.

qa.q: What made Kalyani's three comparisons useful?
qa.a: They came from separate sources, another supplier, a public purchase price and last year's order, so none of them was pulled by the supplier's opening number.

qa.q: How does Arnab see Kalyani's approach?
qa.a: Arnab expected her to bargain down from the opening like most new staff, and is impressed enough to ask her to teach the method to the team.

grounding: Shows a young professional asking what she would pay without the supplier's first figure and collecting three independent comparisons before deciding.

passage:
Thursday night
Omkar's studio quoted ₹90,000 for Tai's engagement photos. My first reaction: okay, maybe we can get it to 75. Then I stopped. Would I have guessed 75 if nobody had said 90? No idea! So I did the boring thing. Called two other photographers that Tai's friends had used: 45 and 55 for the same hours. Also asked Tushar, who shoots weddings in Nashik, what's normal. He said 50 is fair and 90 is "big-hotel pricing". Told Aai. She laughed and said I'm the only daughter who does homework for a party. Booked the 55 one; her candid shots are lovely. Weird how 75 felt cheap this morning.
Charu

qa.q: What did the two other photographers charge for the same hours?
qa.a: They charged 45 and 55 for the same hours.

qa.q: Why did Charu stop after thinking of 75?
qa.a: She realised 75 only came to mind because Omkar's studio had said 90 first, and she wanted to know the fair price without that number in her head.

qa.q: What would you advise a friend who gets a high first quote, based on Charu's day?
qa.a: Pause before countering, ask what you would guess with no quote at all, and collect two or three separate prices or opinions, like Charu's calls and Tushar's view, before deciding. 👍

qa.q: How might Omkar's studio see losing the booking?
qa.a: The studio may be surprised, since a high opening usually leads to bargaining near it; this time the customer came back with outside prices and went elsewhere.

grounding: Shows a young woman noticing that her counter-offer was pulled by the first quote, then resetting by gathering independent prices before booking.

passage: At the Thursday haat in Pipariya, Lakshmi stood before the trader's two goats with her self-help group's money tied in her dupatta. "Eighteen thousand for the pair," the trader said, "and I'm giving you a good rate." Lakshmi felt her mind start to bargain from there: sixteen, maybe fifteen. She stopped. If he hadn't said eighteen, what would she think these goats were worth? She didn't know. "I'll come back," she said. Her friend Sangeeta raised an eyebrow. "He might sell them." "Then he sells them." Together they walked the rows. A man near the banyan tree was asking eleven for a similar pair. Sangeeta's cousin, who kept goats in the next village, said on the phone that ten to twelve was fair this season. Lakshmi went back with her own figure. She bought the pair for twelve.

qa.q: How much did the trader first ask for the pair of goats?
qa.a: Eighteen thousand for the pair.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi say "I'll come back" even though the goats might be sold?
qa.a: She realised her bargaining was starting from the trader's eighteen, not from any real knowledge. She preferred to risk losing the goats than to spend the group's money on his number.

qa.q: Which step made Lakshmi's final price fair?
qa.a: Getting two separate comparisons, the man near the banyan tree and Sangeeta's cousin, before going back. That gave her a figure that did not depend on the first price.

qa.q: How might the other women in Lakshmi's self-help group feel about how she spent their money?
qa.a: They would likely trust her more, since she saved thousands by checking prices rather than accepting a trader's opening figure.

grounding: At a village market, a young woman stops bargaining from a trader's first price, asks what she would judge without it, and checks two other prices.

passage: "Three weeks, tops," said Xin, the lead developer, leaning back. The clinic's booking system in Durban had to move to new servers, and Lindiwe had to give the board a date by Friday. Three weeks already sounded like a fact. That evening she wrote at the top of a page: If nobody had said three, what would I guess? She didn't fully trust her answer, so she gathered comparisons. The pharmacy team's move last year took seven weeks. A friend at another clinic said theirs took six. The vendor's own case notes said five to eight. On Friday she told the board six to eight weeks and explained where each number came from. Xin grumbled, then admitted, "I was thinking of the easy part."

qa.q: How long did the pharmacy team's move take last year?
qa.a: Seven weeks.

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe not trust her own first guess?
qa.a: She felt uneasy that Xin's three weeks was already sitting in her head like a fact, so she wanted numbers that did not start from it.

qa.a: She asked what she would judge without the first figure, then checked three separate sources before giving the board a range.

passage: At the community centre office, the caterer tapped his notebook. "For a health camp like this, you'll need three hundred plates." Kavitha, the new coordinator, nearly wrote 300 on the order form. Then she stopped and turned the form over. "Give me until four o'clock," she said. She asked herself what she would order if nobody had said three hundred. Then she looked for her own numbers. The registration sheet showed 140 names. Last year's camp register showed 170 people had come. And Tenzin, who ran the camp in the next ward, said they had fed about 150 with a few extra. At four she rang the caterer. "One eighty, please." Tenzin grinned when she told him. "Last year someone ordered three hundred. We ate rice for a week."

qa.q: How many names were on the registration sheet?
qa.a: The registration sheet showed 140 names.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha turn the order form over?
qa.a: She felt wary that the caterer's three hundred was about to become her number without any checking, so she wanted to think without it in front of her.

qa.q: Which sources did Kavitha use, and why does using several help?
qa.a: The registration sheet, last year's register and Tenzin's camp; separate figures that agree near 150 to 170 are safer than one opening number.

qa.q: What is it like for Tenzin to hear her final order?
qa.a: Tenzin seems amused and pleased, remembering the year someone ordered three hundred and they ate rice for a week.

grounding: A coordinator sets aside a caterer's first figure and checks three independent numbers before placing the order.

passage:
Dear Minakshi,
You asked how the new job is going. Mostly well! One small thing from this week I want to tell you about. I had to score the interns' final reports, and my senior had already scribbled 4/10 on the corner of Rafiq's. The moment I saw it, everything I read looked like a four. So I stopped, covered the corner with a sticky note, and asked myself what I would give it if I had never seen that number. Then I put it next to two other reports I had already marked, and read the rubric again, line by line. It came out a seven, honestly, because his data section was the best of the three. I wrote a short note explaining why and gave it to my senior. She read it and changed hers to a six.
Miss you. Come to Pune soon.
Sunaina

qa.q: What score had the senior written on Rafiq's report?
qa.a: 4/10, scribbled on the corner.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina cover the corner with a sticky note?
qa.a: Sunaina felt uneasy that the four was colouring everything read afterwards, and wanted to judge the report fairly without it.

qa.q: What steps helped Sunaina reset the score?
qa.a: Asking what score it would get without the four, comparing it with two already-marked reports, and rereading the rubric line by line.

qa.q: How might Rafiq be affected by Sunaina's re-check?
qa.a: Rafiq's strong data section gets fair credit instead of being judged against a quick first mark.

grounding: A young worker hides a senior's first score, asks what the report deserves on its own and compares it with other marked reports.

A Monday in October. Anjali visited the first wedding hall for her sister's reception in Indore. The manager said, "Three lakh for the evening." Anjali felt the number settle in her head like a stone. Anything under three would feel cheap now. She caught herself and wrote in her phone: What would I think this is worth if I'd never heard three lakh?

That Thursday. With her friend Nirmala, she visited two more halls and called a third. Two lakh, two-twenty, two-forty. Nirmala added the cost her cousin had paid last year. The numbers told a different story.

The next Monday. Anjali went back to the first hall with her list. "The others are between two and two-forty." The manager hesitated, then offered two-thirty. Anjali said she'd decide after comparing the food menus too. Walking out, Nirmala grinned. "You didn't even blink at three."

qa.q: How much did the first wedding hall quote?
qa.a: Three lakh for the evening.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel when she heard three lakh, and what did she do with that feeling?
qa.a: She felt the number settle like a stone, sensing anything below would feel cheap, and she caught that feeling and wrote a question to reset her thinking.

qa.q: What made Anjali's decision stronger?
qa.a: Asking what she'd judge without the first figure, then collecting three other quotes and a past cost before deciding.

qa.q: How does Nirmala see Anjali's approach?
qa.a: Nirmala seems amused and proud, noticing Anjali wasn't pulled by the first number.

grounding: It shows a wise decider who asks what she'd judge without the first figure and gathers independent comparisons before deciding, over several days.

passage:
Trisha, you're about to sign for that flat because they came down from thirty to twenty-six? Wait. Let your Seema maasi tell you something.

When I was twenty-four I wanted to buy a sewing machine for my tailoring work, a big industrial one. The first shop said eighty thousand. The owner smiled and said, "For you, seventy." I nearly paid. Seventy felt like a gift.

On the bus home, I asked myself: if I had never heard eighty, what would I think seventy was? I had no idea. That was the frightening part.

So the next week I visited two other shops in Surat and asked a tailor friend what she had paid. The same machine was fifty-five, fifty-eight, and she'd got hers for fifty-two.

I bought it for fifty-five. So, beta, before you sign, who else have you asked?

qa.q: What did the first shop say the sewing machine cost?
qa.a: The first shop said eighty thousand.

qa.q: What did young Seema feel when she realised she had no idea what seventy was worth?
qa.a: Young Seema felt frightened, because seventy had felt like a gift only because of the eighty she had just heard.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Seema's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Asking on the bus what she would think without the first figure, then checking two other shops and a friend, gave her independent comparisons to decide from.

qa.q: How might the first shop owner have seen young Seema's visit?
qa.a: The owner probably expected an easy sale, since offering seventy after eighty makes the lower price feel generous.

grounding: An elder recalls asking what she would think without the first price and gathering independent comparisons before buying.

passage:
The school's annual trip to Pelling was in three days, and the internet in the Gangtok office had been down since morning. Pema, the school's young admin officer, had one bus quote on her desk from Baljeet's travels: ninety-five thousand.

Baljeet phoned. "For the school, I'll make it eighty-five. But confirm today."

Eighty-five sounded reasonable next to ninety-five. Pema almost said yes. Then she stopped herself. If I'd never seen ninety-five, would eighty-five look right?

She honestly didn't know. So she walked to the post office, which had a phone line that worked, and called two other operators and the principal of a nearby school that had done the same trip last year.

The quotes were sixty-eight and seventy-two. The other school had paid seventy.

At four, she called Baljeet back. "Our range is seventy. Can you match it?" After a long pause, he said yes.

qa.q: Where did Pema walk to make phone calls?
qa.a: She walked to the post office, which had a phone line that worked.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she almost said yes to eighty-five?
qa.a: Pema felt relieved and tempted, since eighty-five sounded reasonable next to ninety-five, but then uneasy that she didn't really know.

qa.q: What steps did Pema take, and why were they wise?
qa.a: Pema asked what she would think without the first figure, then got two other quotes and one school's past price, so her decision rested on independent comparisons.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt during the long pause?
qa.a: Baljeet may have felt caught off guard and a little disappointed, knowing his first figure no longer set the terms.

grounding: Under time pressure and a broken connection, a young administrator resets her reference point by gathering independent quotes.

passage:
Zainab had been freelancing as an illustrator for eight months when Damini, who ran a small publishing house in Hyderabad, emailed her: "We'd love you for our children's book. We can offer twelve thousand for the full set of drawings."

Twelve thousand felt like a lot. It was more than her last job. Zainab's hand hovered over the reply button.

Then she sat back. What would I think this job was worth if Damini had never mentioned a number?

She counted the pages: twenty-four illustrations, full colour. She messaged three illustrators she knew from art school and asked, honestly, what they would charge for that. She also checked the rates page of an illustrators' association.

The answers came back: thirty, thirty-five, twenty-eight. The association's range was similar.

Zainab wrote back politely, explaining the scope and suggesting thirty. Damini replied the next day: "Fair. Let's talk at twenty-eight?"

qa.q: How many illustrations did the children's book need?
qa.a: Twenty-four illustrations, full colour.

qa.q: Why did twelve thousand first feel like a lot to Zainab?
qa.a: Zainab felt pleased and tempted because it was more than her last job, and she had no other figure to compare it with yet.

qa.q: What could another freelancer learn from how Zainab replied?
qa.a: Before answering, ask what the work is worth without the first figure, then check two or three independent sources like peers and an association.

qa.q: How might Damini see Zainab after the polite counter-offer?
qa.a: Damini may see Zainab as a professional who knows her worth, and respect her more for it.

grounding: A young freelancer asks what a job is worth without the client's first figure and gathers independent comparisons before replying.

"The seller wants forty thousand for the second-hand scooter," Elizabeth said, reading the message aloud. "You could offer thirty-five and feel great."
Aparna shook her head. "Wait. If I'd never heard forty, what would I think it's worth?"
"No idea. That's why he gave a number."
"Exactly. So let's find out without his number." She opened her laptop. "Same model, same year. Let's find three others."
They scrolled. One listing said twenty-eight. A mechanic friend, on the phone, said twenty-five to thirty for that condition. Another listing was thirty-one.
"So thirty-five isn't a great deal," Elizabeth said slowly.
"It's just a smaller version of his number." Aparna closed the laptop. "I'll offer twenty-eight and explain why. If he says no, there are others."
Elizabeth laughed. "You'd have paid thirty-five yesterday."
"Yesterday I only had his number."

qa.q: What price did the seller first ask for the scooter?
qa.a: The seller asked forty thousand.

qa.q: Why does Aparna refuse to start from the seller's forty?
qa.a: She feels wary of letting his number set her sense of value, so she wants to judge the scooter as if she had never heard it.

qa.q: What steps did Aparna take before deciding, and why do they work?
qa.a: She asked what she would think without the first figure and gathered three independent comparisons, a mechanic's view and two listings, so her offer rests on evidence.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth's view of thirty-five change during the conversation?
qa.a: Elizabeth first sees thirty-five as a good offer, then realises it is only a smaller version of the seller's number.

grounding: It shows a decider asking what she would judge without the first figure and gathering independent comparisons before making an offer.
